items.stem: Historians have offered several reasons why the French monarchy faced bankruptcy by 1787. A: The parlements blocked attempts at reform. items.stem: By 1788 interest payments on the French royal debt took about half of government spending. ‘The French Revolution was caused mainly by the financial crisis of the monarchy.’ Discuss. In your answer you may wish to consider: the royal debt; social grievances.
items.answer: For: Bankruptcy forced the crown to call the Estates-General, the event that opened the revolution. Calonne's and Brienne's failed reforms showed the crisis could not be solved within the old system. The cost of the American war made the debt unmanageable. Against: Enlightenment ideas undermined belief in absolute monarchy and privilege. Resentment of privilege by the bourgeoisie and peasantry created social tension. Poor harvests and high bread prices in 1788-89 brought ordinary people into action. Louis XVI's weak and indecisive leadership turned a crisis into a revolution. Judgement: the financial crisis was the trigger that made change unavoidable, but it became a revolution because of long-term resentment of privilege and new ideas about sovereignty.

items.stem: In August 1788 Louis XVI agreed to summon the Estates-General for May 1789. How far was Louis XVI responsible for the outbreak of revolution in 1789?
items.answer: For: He failed to support reforming ministers such as Turgot and Calonne. He hesitated over the voting dispute and then appeared to threaten the Assembly with troops. His dismissal of Necker in July 1789 provoked the Paris rising. Against: He inherited a debt and a tax system created by earlier kings. The privileged orders and parlements blocked reform. Economic crisis and harvest failure were beyond his control. Judgement: Louis did not cause the crisis, but his indecision at key moments turned a financial crisis into a political revolution.

items.stem: ‘War was the main reason why the revolution became more radical between 1792 and 1794.’ How far do you agree with this view?
items.answer: For: War made the king appear a traitor and led to the overthrow of the monarchy. Defeats and invasion in 1793 justified emergency measures such as the Committee of Public Safety. Conscription provoked the Vendée revolt, which led to brutal repression. Against: The king's own actions, such as the flight to Varennes, undermined constitutional monarchy before war began. Economic crisis and sans-culotte pressure forced measures like the Maximum. Jacobin ideology and the politics of faction drove the Great Terror after the military crisis had eased. Judgement: war was the main catalyst because it linked opposition to treason, but radicalisation also depended on the failure of the king and on sans-culotte pressure.

items.stem: To what extent did the sans-culottes control the course of the revolution in 1792-94?
items.answer: For: They stormed the Tuileries in August 1792. Their rising of 2 June 1793 forced the purge of the Girondins. Their pressure in September 1793 brought the Maximum and put Terror on the agenda. Against: The Jacobin leadership used them and then curbed them, executing the Hébertists in March 1794. The Committee of Public Safety centralised power from late 1793. They had little influence on war strategy or the coup of Thermidor. Judgement: the sans-culottes drove key turning points in 1792-93, but from late 1793 the revolutionary government controlled and then suppressed them.

items.stem: ‘Napoleon preserved the main gains of the revolution.’ How far do you agree?
items.answer: For: The Civil Code kept equality before the law and the end of feudalism. The land settlement and the sale of Church lands were guaranteed. Careers were open to talent in the army and administration. Against: Political liberty disappeared: press censorship, police and a powerless legislature. The Concordat restored the Church's position and a new imperial nobility was created. Women's rights and workers' rights were reduced. Judgement: Napoleon preserved the social gains of 1789 that benefited the propertied classes, but he destroyed political liberty.

items.stem: Explain one reason why the French monarchy faced bankruptcy by 1787.
items.answer: The cost of wars, especially the American war of 1778-83, was paid for by borrowing.
items.markingKey: For each reason: 1 mark for identifying it and 1 mark for explaining it with supporting detail, from: The cost of wars, especially the American war of 1778-83, was paid for by borrowing. Interest on the debt took a growing share of revenue. The privileged orders were largely exempt from direct taxes, so the tax base was narrow. Tax collection through tax farmers was inefficient and corrupt. The parlements blocked attempts at reform. [2]

items.stem: Historians have offered several reasons why the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly in June 1789. A: The dispute over voting by order or by head deadlocked the Estates-General. B: Pamphlets such as Sieyès's What is the Third Estate? encouraged deputies to claim to represent the nation. C: Some clergy joined the Third Estate, strengthening its claim. Explain which of these was the most important reason.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: The dispute over voting by order or by head deadlocked the Estates-General. B: Pamphlets such as Sieyès's What is the Third Estate? encouraged deputies to claim to represent the nation. C: Some clergy joined the Third Estate, strengthening its claim. Possible judgement: the voting deadlock was the immediate trigger, but Enlightenment ideas of popular sovereignty gave the deputies the confidence to act.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: Historians have offered several reasons why Louis XVI agreed to call the Estates-General in 1788. A: The aristocratic revolt of 1788 and riots such as the Day of the Tiles in Grenoble showed resistance to royal authority. B: The treasury suspended payments in August 1788, so the crown had no other way to raise money. C: The Assembly of Notables refused to approve Calonne's land tax in 1787. Which was the most significant? Explain your answer with reference to the other reasons.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: The aristocratic revolt of 1788 and riots such as the Day of the Tiles in Grenoble showed resistance to royal authority. B: The treasury suspended payments in August 1788, so the crown had no other way to raise money. C: The Assembly of Notables refused to approve Calonne's land tax in 1787. Possible judgement: the crown ran out of credit and the privileged orders refused reform, so the king had no alternative.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: To what extent did the Enlightenment cause the French Revolution?
items.answer: For: It spread criticism of absolutism, privilege and the Church. Ideas of popular sovereignty and natural rights shaped the demands of 1789. The American Revolution showed Enlightenment ideas in action. Against: Most philosophes favoured reform, not revolution. Financial bankruptcy forced the calling of the Estates-General. Peasants and urban workers acted mainly because of hunger and feudal dues. Judgement: the Enlightenment shaped how the crisis was understood and what the revolutionaries demanded, but it did not by itself cause the collapse of royal authority.

items.stem: What is meant by “sans-culottes”?
options: The wealthy landowners and officials on whose support Napoleon's regime relied.
The order created in 1802 to reward service to the state, both civil and military.
The single code of French law introduced in 1804, later known as the Code Napoléon.
Radical Parisian artisans, shopkeepers and workers who wore trousers rather than the knee-breeches of the wealthy.

items.stem: Which of these events happened last?
options: The Law of Suspects was passed
The monarchy was overthrown in Paris
The royal family attempted to flee and was stopped at Varennes
items.answer: The Law of Suspects was passed

items.stem: Consider the following explanations of why the Terror was introduced in 1793. A: Civil war in the Vendée and federalist revolts threatened the Republic. B: The Jacobins needed sans-culotte support against the Girondins. C: Food shortages and inflation of the assignat fuelled sans-culotte pressure. Explain how these reasons were linked and decide which mattered most.
items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: Civil war in the Vendée and federalist revolts threatened the Republic. B: The Jacobins needed sans-culotte support against the Girondins. C: Food shortages and inflation of the assignat fuelled sans-culotte pressure. Possible judgement: the Terror began as an emergency response to war and civil war, but it was driven forward by sans-culotte pressure and Jacobin ideology.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a choice; up to 3 marks for explaining it with precise detail; up to 2 marks for comparing it with the other reasons [6]

items.stem: ‘War was the main reason why the revolution became more radical between 1792 and 1794.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: War made the king appear a traitor and led to the overthrow of the monarchy. Defeats and invasion in 1793 justified emergency measures such as the Committee of Public Safety. Conscription provoked the Vendée revolt, which led to brutal repression. Against: The king's own actions, such as the flight to Varennes, undermined constitutional monarchy before war began. Economic crisis and sans-culotte pressure forced measures like the Maximum. Jacobin ideology and the politics of faction drove the Great Terror after the military crisis had eased. Judgement: war was the main catalyst because it linked opposition to treason, but radicalisation also depended on the failure of the king and on sans-culotte pressure.

items.stem: On 18-19 Brumaire (9-10 November 1799) Bonaparte took part in a coup against the Directory. ‘Bonaparte came to power in 1799 mainly because of the weakness of the Directory.’ Discuss.
items.answer: For: The Directory had no stable majority and overturned elections, so it lacked legitimacy. Corruption and economic problems made it unpopular. Defeats in 1799 created a sense of crisis. Against: Bonaparte's military reputation from Italy and his propaganda made him uniquely popular. Sieyès and other politicians planned the coup and chose Bonaparte. The army's loyalty to Bonaparte made the coup possible when the deputies resisted. Judgement: the Directory's weakness created the opportunity, but Bonaparte's reputation and army support explain why he, rather than Sieyès, emerged as master of France.

items.stem: Explain why Napoleon's regime had wide support among the notables.
items.answer: He guaranteed the land settlement of the revolution. The Civil Code protected property and the authority of fathers. Order and efficient administration followed years of instability. Judgement: Napoleon kept the support of the notables mainly because he protected property and offered order and careers.

items.stem: Noah is planning an answer to the question: “‘The French Revolution was caused mainly by the financial crisis of the monarchy.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Noah could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: the financial crisis was the trigger that made change unavoidable, but it became a revolution because of long-term resentment of privilege and new ideas about sovereignty. Support: Bankruptcy forced the crown to call the Estates-General, the event that opened the revolution. Calonne's and Brienne's failed reforms showed the crisis could not be solved within the old system. Challenge: Enlightenment ideas undermined belief in absolute monarchy and privilege. Resentment of privilege by the bourgeoisie and peasantry created social tension.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for a line of argument that answers the question directly and is sustainable; 1 mark for each relevant supporting point and 1 for each challenging point [6]

items.stem: Study all the sources. Source A: a cahier de doléances of a rural parish, spring 1789 (illustrative). “We pay the taille, the tithe and the dues of the lord, while those who own the most pay least. We ask that all subjects bear taxes equally and that the lord's rights over our harvest be abolished.” Source B: a pamphlet by the Abbé Sieyès, What is the Third Estate?, January 1789 (abridged). “What is the Third Estate? Everything. What has it been until now in the political order? Nothing. What does it ask? To become something.” Source C: a report to the king by his finance minister, 1787 (illustrative). “The debt grows each year; the loans of the last war must be paid; the revenues are pledged in advance. Without a tax that falls on all landowners, without exception, the state cannot continue.” “The French Revolution was caused mainly by the financial crisis of the monarchy.” How far do Sources A, B and C support this view?
items.answer: Source A challenges: it shows that social grievances about privilege, not only state finance, drove demands for change. Evaluation: they were often drafted by local lawyers and may not reflect every villager's view. Source B challenges: it presents the revolution as a demand for political rights rather than a response to bankruptcy. Evaluation: it is a piece of political propaganda written to win support. Source C supports: it shows bankruptcy as the central problem facing the monarchy. Evaluation: a minister had reasons to exaggerate the crisis to win support for his plan. Grouping: support C; challenge A, B. A judgement must weigh how convincing each group is, using provenance and own knowledge, rather than counting sources.
items.markingKey: Level 5 (17-20): evaluates the sources (provenance, purpose, context, cross-reference) to show how far they support AND challenge the view, reaching a supported judgement. Level 4 (13-16): uses the sources to support AND challenge the view and evaluates some of them. Level 3 (9-12): uses the sources at face value to support AND challenge. Level 2 (5-8): uses the sources to support OR challenge. Level 1 (1-4): writes about the topic without valid use of the sources. (The examination version uses four sources and 25 marks; levels are scaled.) [20]

The agreement of 1801 between Napoleon and Pope Pius VII that recognised Catholicism as the religion of the majority of the French.
Members of the radical political club that dominated the Convention in 1793-94 under Robespierre.
The royalist rising in Paris in October 1795, put down by troops under Bonaparte.

Napoleon restored the property and privileges of the nobility as they had been before 1789.
The coup of Brumaire went entirely according to plan.

items.stem: Historians have offered several reasons why Robespierre fell from power in July 1794. A: Robespierre had alienated both the Hébertists and Dantonists by executing their leaders. items.answer: Any reasoned choice. A: Robespierre had alienated both the Hébertists and Dantonists by executing their leaders. B: Military victory at Fleurus in June 1794 removed the case for emergency rule. C: The Law of 22 Prairial and the Great Terror made deputies fear for their own lives. Possible judgement: once the military emergency was over, fear among the deputies themselves made it possible to unite against him.

items.stem: How far was the Terror a response to the circumstances of 1793?
items.answer: For: Foreign invasion, civil war and federalist revolts threatened the Republic. Emergency measures such as the levée en masse and the Law of Suspects followed military crisis. Against: The Terror intensified after the military situation improved, with the Law of 22 Prairial in June 1794. Ideas of virtue and the general will justified purging enemies. Factional rivalry led to the execution of Hébertists and Dantonists. Judgement: the Terror began as a response to circumstances, but its peak in 1794 owed more to ideology and factional politics.

items.stem: How successful was the Directory in governing France, 1795-99?
items.answer: For: It survived threats from royalists and the left for four years. It ended the Terror and restored some order. Military victories in Italy brought wealth and territory. Against: It relied on coups such as Fructidor to stay in power. It never solved the financial crisis or inflation. It was overthrown in 1799 with little resistance. Judgement: it achieved survival and some stability after the Terror, but its dependence on the army made it a failure as a constitutional government.

items.stem: Kwame is planning an answer to the question: “‘Napoleon preserved the main gains of the revolution.’ How far do you agree?” Write a one-sentence line of argument for the answer and outline two points Kwame could use to support the view and two to challenge it.
items.answer: Line of argument: Napoleon preserved the social gains of 1789 that benefited the propertied classes, but he destroyed political liberty. Support: The Civil Code kept equality before the law and the end of feudalism. The land settlement and the sale of Church lands were guaranteed. Challenge: Political liberty disappeared: press censorship, police and a powerless legislature. The Concordat restored the Church's position and a new imperial nobility was created.
